title: Earth Lost 11 Trillion Tons of Ice in 47 Years
paragraphs: The giant ice sheets covering Greenland and Antarctica have lost more than 11 trillion metric tons of ice over the past 47 years, according to a major new study based on satellite data.

The study, which was published in the journal Scientific Data in September 2026, was carried out by an international team led by the European Space Agency. By combining data from European and NASA satellites, the researchers were able to reconstruct how the volume of the ice sheets has changed since 1979 in Antarctica and since 1972 in Greenland. In total, they used information from 45 independent surveys and 27 different satellites.

The researchers found that around 11.3 trillion metric tons of ice melted between 1979 and 2023. That is enough to cover the entire continental United States with ice about 1.5 meters deep. The meltwater has raised global sea levels by about 3.1 centimeters. Although this may not sound like much, every centimeter of sea level rise exposes another two to three million people around the world to at least one flood a year.

The ice sheets were relatively stable through the 1970s, 1980s and into the 1990s, but melting increased substantially in the 2010s. Most of the loss has been caused by warmer ocean water, which is eating away at the ice sheets from below and from the sides. As a result, glaciers are flowing more quickly into the sea. For instance, the Jakobshavn glacier in Greenland is retreating by up to 50 meters a day.

Interestingly, the rate of ice loss appeared to level off between 2020 and 2023. However, the researchers believe this was caused by short-term weather patterns, such as record snowfall in East Antarctica. According to Inès Otosaka of Northumbria University, the study's lead author, more recent measurements suggest that the acceleration has resumed. Eric Rignot of the University of California, Irvine, one of the co-authors, described the pause as just a bump in the record.

Another co-author, Andrew Shepherd, warned that the ice sheets are responding to global warming with a delay of several decades. This means that the melting will continue even if humans are able to stop heating the planet.
